e.etymology: An Albanian name traced to Latin Laurentius, the source of Laurence. Lorik is also an Armenian name from lor, quail.
The Samoan word malosi, strong or powerful.
A spelling of Kashmir, the Himalayan region that also gave its name to cashmere wool; the C brings out the nickname Cash.

assoc.t: Kashmir, the Himalayan region, spelled with a K
cashmere, the soft luxury wool (same sound)

e.etymology: The Swahili word for lion. In Shona, a language of Zimbabwe, simba means strength and is a common short name.
namesakes: Simba (lion hero of Disney's The Lion King)

assoc.t: the lion hero of Disney's The Lion King

e.etymology: A Hebrew name, also written Yannai, borne by the Hasmonean king Alexander Jannaeus and by Talmudic rabbis. It is usually explained as a short form of Yochanan or from the verb to answer.
The Nahuatl (Aztec) word for blood. It is used in Mexican and Mexican-American families.
A recent American coinage joining Ky-, as in Kyrie and Kyree, to -sir, as in Nasir and Yasir; it also sounds like Kaiser.
A recent name in the sound family of Leilani, Kehlani and Delani, seen mostly in Latino families.
A single-l spelling of Ollivander, the wandmaker's surname in the Harry Potter books, which also reads as Oliver with the ending of Evander and Lysander.

assoc.t: Ollivander, the wandmaker in Harry Potter

e.etymology: The English word for dark volcanic glass, from Latin obsidianus, a misreading of obsianus, the stone that Pliny says a Roman named Obsius found in Ethiopia.
A recent American coinage: Jaylen or Zaylen with an initial X, said as Z.
The Punjabi pronunciation of Zorawar, from Persian zorawar, having zor, strength or force. Sikh families use it in honor of Sahibzada Zorawar Singh, a son of Guru Gobind Singh.
A respelling of Kehlani, itself a modern spelling of the Hawaiian names Kalani, the heavens, and Kailani, sea and sky. Singer Kehlani made that spelling popular after 2015.

e.meaning: uncertain; often given as heart or courageous
e.etymology: A spelling of Tadeo, the Spanish form of Thaddeus, with the Th- of the English name. Thaddeus, one of the twelve apostles, has an Aramaic name of uncertain meaning.
An Old English name made of uht, the hour before dawn, and raed, counsel, borne by 11th-century earls of Northumbria. Bernard Cornwell revived it for the hero of The Last Kingdom.
namesakes: Uhtred of Bebbanburg (warrior hero of The Last Kingdom)

assoc.t: Uhtred of Bebbanburg, hero of The Last Kingdom

e.etymology: A Maya name from ik, wind or breath, glossed as spirit. It is used in Mexico and in Mexican-American families.
A spelling of Kroy or Croy, a Scottish surname and place name; Kroy became known through football player and reality TV figure Kroy Biermann.
Entered US use in 2023 after Kylie Jenner and Travis Scott named their son Aire, said like air and reported to mean lion of God, the sense of Hebrew Ariel. Aire is also an Estonian girls' name.

assoc.t: Aire Webster, son of Kylie Jenner and Travis Scott

e.etymology: A recent American name that follows the sound of Kiyomi, a Japanese name usually written as pure beauty, and of Naomi.
A variant of Dolores, from the Spanish title of the Virgin Mary, María de los Dolores, Mary of the Sorrows. This spelling was popular in the United States in the 1920s and 1930s.

e.meaning: Germanic name ending in the word for peace
e.etymology: A variant of Jeffrey, the usual American spelling of Geoffrey, a Norman French name from Germanic. Its second part is frid, peace; the first is disputed.
The German form of Eric, from Old Norse Eirikr, made of ei, ever or alone, and rikr, ruler.
namesakes: Erich Maria Remarque (author of All Quiet on the Western Front)
Erich Fromm (psychologist and author of The Art of Loving)

e.etymology: A feminine form of Alvin, from Old English Aelfwine, elf friend, or Aethelwine, noble friend.
Mary and Beth, the short form of Elizabeth, written as one word; most popular in the 1950s and 1960s.
A feminine form of John recorded since the 18th century. John goes back to Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious.
An elaboration of Jean, the English form of French Jeanne, a feminine form of John; often said like Gina.

e.meaning: pet form of Melissa, Greek for bee
e.etymology: A pet form of Melissa, from Greek melissa, honeybee; also simply the affectionate word missy, little miss.
An African-American coinage that joins the Ra- prefix to Shaun, the Irish form of John; also spelled Rashawn and Rashon.
A variant of Christiana, the Latin feminine of Christian, follower of Christ.
The German, Polish and Scandinavian spelling of Angelica, from Latin angelicus, angelic, which goes back to Greek angelos, messenger.
A spelling of Jamel, a form of the Arabic names Jamal, beauty, and Jamil, handsome, used in African-American families since the 1970s.
A US name in the family of Jacques and Jaquan, said juh-KWEZ like Marquez. Jáquez is also a Spanish surname.
